title: A simple but effective model for attachment in discourse parsing with multi-task learning for relation labeling
research_question: Can a relatively simple BERT-based local discourse parser jointly exploit attachment and relation-label information while supporting the multiple-parent structures required by multiparty conversation?
methodology: The authors train BERTLine on versions of the STAC multiparty game-chat corpus, encoding pairs of elementary discourse units with BERT and adding speaker-change and discourse-distance features. Attachment is treated as binary prediction over candidate parents among the preceding ten discourse units, while relation labeling uses a multi-task BERT model with separate attachment and 16-way discourse-relation heads. Predictions are evaluated with micro-averaged F1, explicitly including structures with multiple parents, and are compared with reimplemented prior discourse parsers. The authors also construct STAC-Squished by collapsing predictable adjacent game-event chains in the situated STAC data and perform ablations over structural information and multi-task learning.

key_findings.finding: The STAC discourse formalism directly permits a single discourse unit to attach to multiple earlier units, reflecting cases in which one conversational move responds to several prior moves at once.

BERTLine can predict multiple parents rather than forcing a tree, but it recovered only about 20% of the 77 multi-parent structures in the reported test set, including a small number with more than three parents.
Question–Answer-Pair is one of the 16 relation labels represented in the STAC graphs, so question/answer linkage is modeled as one discourse-relation type inside a more general attachment graph.

On standard STAC, BERTLine obtained about 73.1 attachment F1 and 56.25 relation-label F1 and was competitive with or better than the reimplemented neural alternatives, particularly for relation labeling.

Joint multi-task training of attachment and relation labeling improved relation F1 by about one point relative to the authors' pipeline formulation, supporting interdependence between deciding whether units connect and deciding how they connect.

The authors found substantial data-quality problems in standard STAC, including 488 duplicate EDUs across 60 dialogues and many Continuation relations whose interpretation becomes problematic when nonlinguistic game actions are omitted.

STAC-Squished increased the reported overall attachment and relation scores, while the authors caution that situated data can make aggregate results look better because easily predicted event-event links dominate harder linguistic attachments.

limitations: Only the preceding ten discourse units are considered as candidate parents, imposing a fixed locality bound that can exclude longer-range reply dependencies.
Although the architecture permits multiple parents, it captures only about one fifth of the annotated multi-parent structures in the reported test data.
Results aggregate relation types; the paper does not provide Question–Answer-Pair-specific precision, recall, or F1, so performance on replies to questions cannot be isolated.
STAC consists of multiparty online game chats rather than email, and the authors explicitly note uncertainty about transfer to spoken conversation and other discourse domains.
The standard STAC data contain duplicated units and discourse-label inconsistencies, while the situated version contains easy event-event chains that can inflate aggregate scores.
The newly constructed STAC-Squished corpus had not yet received the detailed error analysis and cross-corpus validation that the authors considered necessary.

The model represents attachment between discourse units but does not explicitly distinguish complete answers, partial answers, unanswered questions, or which proposition within a multi-proposition question was addressed.
raw_claims: Multiparty conversational structure is not necessarily a tree because a single turn can react to several preceding moves.
STAC represents discourse as a directed acyclic graph with labeled relations between elementary discourse units.
Question–Answer-Pair is one of the discourse relations predicted by the parser.
The attachment model independently scores several preceding units, which allows more than one parent to be selected.
Only about 20% of the test-set multi-parent structures were recovered by the reported system.
Multi-task learning couples attachment information with relation classification and modestly improves relation labeling.
Standard STAC contains duplicated dialogue material and relations affected by omitted game-state information.
Situated STAC contains numerous easily predicted adjacent event links that can distort aggregate evaluation.
STAC-Squished collapses chains of predictable nonlinguistic events and is released with the authors' implementation.
The paper does not report separate empirical results for Question–Answer-Pair links or unanswered-question behavior.
